source.author: stat
source.text: monstrat enim suadetque timor; stupet anxius alto corda metu glaciante pater: Trinacria qualis ora repercussum Libyco mare sumit ab aestu, mox plenum Phoebo vatem et celerare iubentem nunc humilis genua amplectens, nunc ora canentis nequiquam reticere rogat; iam fama sacratam vocem amplexa volat, clamavitque oracula Thebae.
source.text_original: monstrat enim suadetque timor; stupet anxius alto / corda metu glaciante pater: Trinacria qualis / ora repercussum Libyco mare sumit ab aestu, / mox plenum Phoebo vatem et celerare iubentem / nunc humilis genua amplectens, nunc ora canentis / nequiquam reticere rogat; iam fama sacratam / vocem amplexa volat, clamavitque oracula Thebae.
source.text_english: For fear both points out and urges him; the father, anxious, is stunned, his heart freezing with deep dread: as the Trinacrian shore receives the sea rebounding from the Libyan surf, and soon, the prophet, filled with Phoebus and bidding him hurry on, now clasping his knees in humility, now begging him in vain to keep silent as he sings; already rumor, having seized upon the sacred voice, flies, and Thebae cried out the oracles.

reuse.text: Minyas ambage ducemque terrificat; sed enim contra Phoebeius Idmon, non pallore viris, non ullo horrore comarum terribilis, plenus fatis Phoeboque quieto, cui genitor tribuit monitu praenoscere divum omina, seu flammas seu lubrica comminus exta seu plenum certis interroget aera pennis, sic sociis Mopsoque canit:
reuse.text_original: Minyas ambage ducemque / terrificat; sed enim contra Phoebeius Idmon, / non pallore viris, non ullo horrore comarum / terribilis, plenus fatis Phoeboque quieto, / cui genitor tribuit monitu praenoscere divum / omina, seu flammas seu lubrica comminus exta / seu plenum certis interroget aera pennis, / sic sociis Mopsoque canit:
reuse.text_english: He terrifies the Minyae with a roundabout tale and their leader; but on the other side Phoebus’ Idmon, not dreadful to men with paleness, not with any horrid mane of hair, but full of fate and of a calm Phoebus, to whom his father granted by his warning to know in advance the omens of the gods, whether he asks the flames, or slippery entrails at close range, or the air full of assured wings, thus sings to his companions and to Mopsus:
